question: Let $$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$$ and $$B=\begin{bmatrix}2&p\\q&4\end{bmatrix}.$$ Determine the values of $p$ and $q$ for which $AB=BA$, and hence justify through a suitable choice of non-zero $p$ and $q$ that matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.
explanation:
Formation of the Products

We have $$AB=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&p\\q&4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2&p\\3q&12\end{bmatrix}$$ and $$BA=\begin{bmatrix}2&p\\q&4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2&3p\\q&12\end{bmatrix}$$

Required Condition

For $AB=BA$, corresponding elements must be equal. Therefore, $$p=3p$$ and $$3q=q$$ These give $$2p=0,\quad 2q=0$$ Hence, $$p=0,\quad q=0$$ Thus, the given matrices commute only when $$B=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&4\end{bmatrix}$$

Examination of Non-Commutativity

For example, take $p=1$ and $q=1$. Then $$AB=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\3&12\end{bmatrix}$$ whereas $$BA=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&12\end{bmatrix}$$ Clearly, $AB\ne BA$. Therefore, although some special pairs of matrices may commute, matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.

options.B: $p=0,\ q=0$ are required for $AB=BA$; for example, $p=q=1$ gives $AB\ne BA$
options.C: $p=0,\ q=1$ are required for $AB=BA$; for example, $p=q=1$ gives $AB=BA$
options.D: $p=1,\ q=0$ are required for $AB=BA$; for example, $p=q=1$ gives $AB\ne BA$
